newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland awaits new, smaller flood swell.
newsitem.headline: Poland awaits new, smaller flood swell.

text.p: A new high-water swell advanced up Poland's Odra river on Wednesday but authorities said it was not likely to renew the havoc of the last two weeks which has left over 50,000 people unable to return home.

Flood crisis committee official Marek Sobczak said the latest flood wave would hit the southwestern city of Opole late on Wednesday and would again inundate the residential estate of Zacisze in Wroclaw, further north.

But he said there would be no repeat of the earlier calamity that drowned downtown Opole in two metres of water. "We should not expect another catastrophe on the same scale as early this month," Sobczak said.
He said there would also be new flooding along the Warta river, which had reversed its flow as it merged with the brimming Odra by Kostrzyn on the German border.
Other communities had already fallen victim to the latest rains, which heaped misery on a country still reeling from the effects of downpours more than two weeks ago.
Sobczak said 54 sq km (21 sq miles) had been flooded overnight, with the Czestochowa, Kalisz and above all Wroclaw provinces most affected.
Many of the hundreds of thousands of people whose homes had already been damaged were still waiting for the waters to drain so they could begin to clean up and rebuild.
According to Sobczak 518 communities were still flooded, 12 of them totally, out of a total of 1,278 towns and villages that had been struck by the disaster.
Of the 5,972 sq km of Poland that had been swamped, 2,710 sq km were still under water, while 52,300 evacuees were still unable to return to their homes.
Police said the confirmed death toll in Poland for the entire period of flooding was now 55.
Forecasters said the outlook for the next few days was at least more hopeful.

"In the coming two days we are expecting occasional showers over the area...but there will be no heavy, continual rains," an official of Poland's Meteorology and Water Management Institute said. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
